title: Teaching AI to automate a game trailer recording (take #4)
author: fapfap_ahh
selftext:
Game background - WATCHSTATION: First-person game where you run a lone Soviet-style radar station in any number of locations and decide what to report. 



It's heading for alpha with the first complete location (siberia), so I wanted to learn (together with Claude) how to make a trailer. I directed and gave notes, and Claude built the tooling and did the leg work.



\- The game films itself. A film mode plays "takes" from a spreadsheet: a camera path plus timed commands like spawn a deer or ring the phone

\- It records frame-exact 4K piped into ffmpeg, then replays each take in real time to capture the sound

\- The AI renders test frames of each take headlessly to check framing. Then it asks to take over my screen for the real recording

\- I wrote a section outline and iterated that into 13 scenes for take #4.

\- AI recorded that batch unattended in about 8 minutes.

\- Edits for the trailer happen via scripts too: cuts, section banners, zooms onto UI cards, a music bed, transitions, title cards from a small Python script, all via ffmpeg.

\- My notes ranged from vital scenarios to show gameplay features down to small things like god rays blowing out the sun

\- As noted above, it helped find real bugs as well. The generator caught fire mid-repair because an electrical fault fired. A very low health generator (smoking and catching fire soon) should block you from repair until you douse it with the extinguisher.



Feedback welcome! Plan to iterate on this further.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: I've really enjoyed making trailers for my own game this way. Good work. The bonus I love is "and output to both a portrait view or landscape" or basically outputting video in any ratio, at any quality, and all on a low-end laptop.
